Page 130 \n5.2.1 Prefer using dedicated EKS Service Accounts (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: Kubernetes workloads should not use cluster node service accounts to authenticate to Amazon EKS APIs. Each Kubernetes workload that needs to authenticate to other AWS services using AWS IAM should be provisioned with a dedicated Service account. Rationale: Manual approaches for authenticating Kubernetes workloads running on Amazon EKS against AWS APIs are: storing service account keys as a Kubernetes secret (which introduces manual key rotation and potential for key compromise); or use of the underlying nodes\' IAM Service account, which violates the principle of least privilege on a multi-tenanted node, when one pod needs to have access to a service, but every other pod on the node that uses the Service account does not. Audit: For each namespace in the cluster, review the rights assigned to the default service account and ensure that it has no roles or cluster roles bound to it apart from the defaults. Additionally ensure that the automountServiceAccountToken: false setting is in place for each default service account. Remediation: With IAM roles for service accounts on Amazon EKS clusters, you can associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes service account. This service account can then provide AWS permissions to the containers in any pod that uses that service account. With this feature, you no longer need to provide extended permissions to the worker node IAM role so that pods on that node can call AWS APIs. Applications must sign their AWS API requests with AWS credentials. This feature provides a strategy for managing credentials for your applications, similar to the way that Amazon EC2 instance profiles provide credentials to Amazon EC2 instances. Instead of creating and distributing your AWS credentials to the containers or using the Amazon EC2 instance’s role, you can associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes service account. The applications in the pod’s containers can then use an AWS SDK or the AWS CLI to make API requests to authorized AWS services. The IAM roles for service accounts feature provides the following benefits: • Least privilege — By using the IAM roles for service accounts feature, you no longer need to provide extended permissions to the worker node IAM role so that pods on that node can call AWS APIs. You can scope IAM permissions to a service account, and only pods that use that service account have access to Page 131 \nthose permissions. This feature also eliminates the need for third-party solutions such as kiam or kube2iam. • Credential isolation — A container can only retrieve credentials for the IAM role that is associated with the service account to which it belongs. A container never has access to credentials that are intended for another container that belongs to another pod. • Audit-ability — Access and event logging is available through CloudTrail to help ensure retrospective auditing. To get started, see list text hereEnabling IAM roles for service accounts on your cluster. For an end-to-end walkthrough using eksctl, see Walkthrough: Updating a DaemonSet to use IAM for service accounts. References: 1. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html 2. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts-cni-walkthrough.html 3. https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/security/docs/iam/#scope-the-iam-role-trust-policy-for-irsa-to-the-service-account-name CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 12.8 Establish and Maintain Dedicated Computing Resources for All Administrative Work  Establish and maintain dedicated computing resources, either physically or logically separated, for all administrative tasks or tasks requiring administrative access. The computing resources should be segmented from the enterprise\'s primary network and not be allowed internet access.   ● \nv7 4.3 Ensure the Use of Dedicated Administrative Accounts  Ensure that all users with administrative account access use a dedicated or secondary account for elevated activities. This account should only be used for administrative activities and not internet browsing, email, or similar activities. ● ● ● \n Page 132 \n5.3 AWS EKS Key Management Service This section contains recommendations relating to using AWS EKS Key Management. Page 133 \n5.3.1 Ensure Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted using Customer Master Keys (CMKs) managed in AWS KMS (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: Encrypt Kubernetes secrets, stored in etcd, using secrets encryption feature during Amazon EKS cluster creation. Rationale: Kubernetes can store secrets that pods can access via a mounted volume. Today, Kubernetes secrets are stored with Base64 encoding, but encrypting is the recommended approach. Amazon EKS clusters version 1.13 and higher support the capability of encrypting your Kubernetes secrets using AWS Key Management Service (KMS) Customer Managed Keys (CMK). The only requirement is to enable the encryption provider support during EKS cluster creation. Use AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keys to provide envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets stored in Amazon EKS. Implementing envelope encryption is considered a security best practice for applications that store sensitive data and is part of a defense in depth security strategy. Application-layer Secrets Encryption provides an additional layer of security for sensitive data, such as user defined Secrets and Secrets required for the operation of the cluster, such as service account keys, which are all stored in etcd. Using this functionality, you can use a key, that you manage in AWS KMS, to encrypt data at the application layer. This protects against attackers in the event that they manage to gain access to etcd. Audit: Using the etcdctl commandline, read that secret out of etcd: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/default/secret1 [...] | hexdump -C where [...] must be the additional arguments for connecting to the etcd server. Verify the stored secret is prefixed with k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: which indicates the aescbc provider has encrypted the resulting data. Remediation: This process can only be performed during Cluster Creation. Enable \'Secrets Encryption\' during Amazon EKS cluster creation as described in the links within the \'References\' section. Page 134 \nDefault Value: By default secrets created using the Kubernetes API are stored in tmpfs and are encrypted at rest. References: 1. https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2020/03/amazon-eks-adds-envelope-encryption-for-secrets-with-aws-kms/ CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 3.11 Encrypt Sensitive Data at Rest  Encrypt sensitive data at rest on servers, applications, and databases containing sensitive data. Storage-layer encryption, also known as server-side encryption, meets the minimum requirement of this Safeguard. Additional encryption methods may include application-layer encryption, also known as client-side encryption, where access to the data storage device(s) does not permit access to the plain-text data.   ● ● \nv7 14.8 Encrypt Sensitive Information at Rest  Encrypt all sensitive information at rest using a tool that requires a secondary authentication mechanism not integrated into the operating system, in order to access the information.   ● \n Page 135 \n5.4 Cluster Networking This section contains recommendations relating to network security configurations in Amazon EKS. Page 136 \n5.4.1 Restrict Access to the Control Plane Endpoint (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: Enable Endpoint Private Access to restrict access to the cluster\'s control plane to only an allowlist of authorized IPs. Rationale: Authorized networks are a way of specifying a restricted range of IP addresses that are permitted to access your cluster\'s control plane. Kubernetes Engine uses both Transport Layer Security (TLS) and authentication to provide secure access to your cluster\'s control plane from the public internet. This provides you the flexibility to administer your cluster from anywhere; however, you might want to further restrict access to a set of IP addresses that you control. You can set this restriction by specifying an authorized network. Restricting access to an authorized network can provide additional security benefits for your container cluster, including: • Better protection from outsider attacks: Authorized networks provide an additional layer of security by limiting external access to a specific set of addresses you designate, such as those that originate from your premises. This helps protect access to your cluster in the case of a vulnerability in the cluster\'s authentication or authorization mechanism. • Better protection from insider attacks: Authorized networks help protect your cluster from accidental leaks of master certificates from your company\'s premises. Leaked certificates used from outside Cloud Services and outside the authorized IP ranges (for example, from addresses outside your company) are still denied access. Impact: When implementing Endpoint Private Access, be careful to ensure all desired networks are on the allowlist (whitelist) to prevent inadvertently blocking external access to your cluster\'s control plane. Page 137 \nAudit: Remediation: By enabling private endpoint access to the Kubernetes API server, all communication between your nodes and the API server stays within your VPC. You can also limit the IP addresses that can access your API server from the internet, or completely disable internet access to the API server. With this in mind, you can update your cluster accordingly using the AWS CLI to ensure that Private Endpoint Access is enabled. If you choose to also enable Public Endpoint Access then you should also configure a list of allowable CIDR blocks, resulting in restricted access from the internet. If you specify no CIDR blocks, then the public API server endpoint is able to receive and process requests from all IP addresses by defaulting to [\'0.0.0.0/0\']. For example, the following command would enable private access to the Kubernetes API as well as limited public access over the internet from a single IP address (noting the /32 CIDR suffix): aws eks update-cluster-config --region $AWS_REGION --name $CLUSTER_NAME --resources-vpc-config endpointPrivateAccess=true, endpointPrivateAccess=true, publicAccessCidrs="203.0.113.5/32" Note: The CIDR blocks specified cannot include reserved addresses. There is a maximum number of CIDR blocks that you can specify. For more information, see the EKS Service Quotas link in the references section. For more detailed information, see the EKS Cluster Endpoint documentation link in the references section. Default Value: By default, Endpoint Public Access is disabled. References: 1. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cluster-endpoint.html CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 4.4 Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers  Implement and manage a firewall on servers, where supported. Example implementations include a virtual firewall, operating system firewall, or a third-party firewall agent. ● ● ● \nv8 9.3 Maintain and Enforce Network-Based URL Filters  Enforce and update network-based URL filters to limit an enterprise asset from connecting to potentially malicious or unapproved websites. Example implementations include category-based filtering, reputation-based filtering, or through the use of block lists. Enforce filters for all enterprise assets.  ● ● Page 138 \nControls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv7 7.4 Maintain and Enforce Network-Based URL Filters  Enforce network-based URL filters that limit a system\'s ability to connect to websites not approved by the organization. This filtering shall be enforced for each of the organization\'s systems, whether they are physically at an organization\'s facilities or not.  ● ● \n Page 139 \n5.4.2 Ensure clusters are created with Private Endpoint Enabled and Public Access Disabled (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 2 Description: Disable access to the Kubernetes API from outside the node network if it is not required. Rationale: In a private cluster, the master node has two endpoints, a private and public endpoint. The private endpoint is the internal IP address of the master, behind an internal load balancer in the master\'s VPC network. Nodes communicate with the master using the private endpoint. The public endpoint enables the Kubernetes API to be accessed from outside the master\'s VPC network. Although Kubernetes API requires an authorized token to perform sensitive actions, a vulnerability could potentially expose the Kubernetes publically with unrestricted access. Additionally, an attacker may be able to identify the current cluster and Kubernetes API version and determine whether it is vulnerable to an attack. Unless required, disabling public endpoint will help prevent such threats, and require the attacker to be on the master\'s VPC network to perform any attack on the Kubernetes API. Impact: Configure the EKS cluster endpoint to be private. 1. Leave the cluster endpoint public and specify which CIDR blocks can communicate with the cluster endpoint. The blocks are effectively a whitelisted set of public IP addresses that are allowed to access the cluster endpoint. 2. Configure public access with a set of whitelisted CIDR blocks and set private endpoint access to enabled. This will allow public access from a specific range of public IPs while forcing all network traffic between the kubelets (workers) and the Kubernetes API through the cross-account ENIs that get provisioned into the cluster VPC when the control plane is provisioned. Audit: Check for private endpoint access to the Kubernetes API server Page 140 \nRemediation: By enabling private endpoint access to the Kubernetes API server, all communication between your nodes and the API server stays within your VPC. With this in mind, you can update your cluster accordingly using the AWS CLI to ensure that Private Endpoint Access is enabled. For example, the following command would enable private access to the Kubernetes API and ensure that no public access is permitted: aws eks update-cluster-config --region $AWS_REGION --name $CLUSTER_NAME --resources-vpc-config endpointPrivateAccess=true, endpointPublicAccess=false Note: For more detailed information, see the EKS Cluster Endpoint documentation link in the references section. Default Value: By default, the Public Endpoint is disabled. References: 1. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cluster-endpoint.html CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 4.4 Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers  Implement and manage a firewall on servers, where supported. Example implementations include a virtual firewall, operating system firewall, or a third-party firewall agent. ● ● ● \nv7 12 Boundary Defense  Boundary Defense    \n Page 141 \n5.4.3 Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: Disable public IP addresses for cluster nodes, so that they only have private IP addresses. Private Nodes are nodes with no public IP addresses. Rationale: Disabling public IP addresses on cluster nodes restricts access to only internal networks, forcing attackers to obtain local network access before attempting to compromise the underlying Kubernetes hosts. Impact: To enable Private Nodes, the cluster has to also be configured with a private master IP range and IP Aliasing enabled. Private Nodes do not have outbound access to the public internet. If you want to provide outbound Internet access for your private nodes, you can use Cloud NAT or you can manage your own NAT gateway. Audit: Remediation: aws eks update-cluster-config \\     --region region-code \\     --name my-cluster \\     --resources-vpc-config endpointPublicAccess=true,publicAccessCidrs="203.0.113.5/32",endpointPrivateAccess=true CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 4.4 Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers  Implement and manage a firewall on servers, where supported. Example implementations include a virtual firewall, operating system firewall, or a third-party firewall agent. ● ● ● \nv7 12 Boundary Defense  Boundary Defense    \n Page 142 \n5.4.4 Ensure Network Policy is Enabled and set as appropriate (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: Amazon EKS provides two ways to implement network policy. You choose a network policy option when you create an EKS cluster. The policy option can\'t be changed after the cluster is created: Calico Network Policies, an open-source network and network security solution founded by Tigera. Both implementations use Linux IPTables to enforce the specified policies. Policies are translated into sets of allowed and disallowed IP pairs. These pairs are then programmed as IPTable filter rules. Rationale: By default, all pod to pod traffic within a cluster is allowed. Network Policy creates a pod-level firewall that can be used to restrict traffic between sources. Pod traffic is restricted by having a Network Policy that selects it (through the use of labels). Once there is any Network Policy in a namespace selecting a particular pod, that pod will reject any connections that are not allowed by any Network Policy. Other pods in the namespace that are not selected by any Network Policy will continue to accept all traffic. Network Policies are managed via the Kubernetes Network Policy API and enforced by a network plugin, simply creating the resource without a compatible network plugin to implement it will have no effect. Impact: Network Policy requires the Network Policy add-on. This add-on is included automatically when a cluster with Network Policy is created, but for an existing cluster, needs to be added prior to enabling Network Policy. Enabling/Disabling Network Policy causes a rolling update of all cluster nodes, similar to performing a cluster upgrade. This operation is long-running and will block other operations on the cluster (including delete) until it has run to completion. Enabling Network Policy enforcement consumes additional resources in nodes. Specifically, it increases the memory footprint of the kube-system process by approximately 128MB, and requires approximately 300 millicores of CPU. Audit: Remediation: Default Value: By default, Network Policy is disabled. Page 143 \nCIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 12.6 Use of Secure Network Management and Communication Protocols   Use secure network management and communication protocols (e.g., 802.1X, Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2) Enterprise or greater).  ● ● \nv7 9.2 Ensure Only Approved Ports, Protocols and Services Are Running  Ensure that only network ports, protocols, and services listening on a system with validated business needs, are running on each system.  ● ● \nv7 9.4 Apply Host-based Firewalls or Port Filtering  Apply host-based firewalls or port filtering tools on end systems, with a default-deny rule that drops all traffic except those services and ports that are explicitly allowed. ● ● ● \n Page 144 \n5.4.5 Encrypt traffic to HTTPS load balancers with TLS certificates (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 2 Description: Encrypt traffic to HTTPS load balancers using TLS certificates. Page 146 \n5.5.1 Manage Kubernetes RBAC users with AWS IAM Authenticator for Kubernetes (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 2 Description: Amazon EKS uses IAM to provide authentication to your Kubernetes cluster through the AWS IAM Authenticator for Kubernetes. You can configure the stock kubectl client to work with Amazon EKS by installing the AWS IAM Authenticator for Kubernetes and modifying your kubectl configuration file to use it for authentication. Rationale: On- and off-boarding users is often difficult to automate and prone to error. Using a single source of truth for user permissions reduces the number of locations that an individual must be off-boarded from, and prevents users gaining unique permissions sets that increase the cost of audit. Impact: Users must now be assigned to the IAM group created to use this namespace and deploy applications. If they are not they will not be able to access the namespace or deploy. Audit: To Audit access to the namespace $NAMESPACE, assume the IAM role yourIAMRoleName for a user that you created, and then run the following command: $ kubectl get role -n $NAMESPACE The response lists the RBAC role that has access to this Namespace. Remediation: Refer to the \'Managing users or IAM roles for your cluster\' in Amazon EKS documentation. Note: If using AWS CLI version 1.16.156 or later there is no need to install the AWS IAM Authenticator anymore. The relevant AWS CLI commands, depending on the use case, are: aws eks update-kubeconfig aws eks get-token Default Value: For role-based access control (RBAC), system:masters permissions are configured in the Amazon EKS control plane Page 147 \nReferences: 1. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/add-user-role.html 2. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/add-user-role.html CIS Controls: Controls Version Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 6.8 Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control  Define and maintain role-based access control, through determining and documenting the access rights necessary for each role within the enterprise to successfully carry out its assigned duties. Page 149 \n5.6.1 Consider Fargate for running untrusted workloads (Manual) Profile Applicability: •  Level 1 Description: It is Best Practice to restrict or fence untrusted workloads when running in a multi-tenant environment. Rationale: Audit: Remediation: Create a Fargate profile for your cluster Before you can schedule pods running on Fargate in your cluster, you must define a Fargate profile that specifies which pods should use Fargate when they are launched. For more information, see AWS Fargate profile. Note If you created your cluster with eksctl using the --fargate option, then a Fargate profile has already been created for your cluster with selectors for all pods in the kube-system and default namespaces. Use the following procedure to create Fargate profiles for any other namespaces you would like to use with Fargate. via eksctl CLI Create your Fargate profile with the following eksctl command, replacing the variable text with your own values. You must specify a namespace, but the labels option is not required. eksctl create fargateprofile --cluster cluster_name --name fargate_profile_name --namespace kubernetes_namespace --labels key=value via AWS Management Console To create a Fargate profile for a cluster with the AWS Management Console 1. Open the Amazon EKS console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/eks/home#/clusters. 2. Choose the cluster to create a Fargate profile for. 3. Under Fargate profiles, choose Add Fargate profile. 4. On the Configure Fargate profile page, enter the following information and choose Next. • For Name, enter a unique name for your Fargate profile. • For Pod execution role, choose the pod execution role to use with your Fargate profile. Only IAM roles with the eks-fargate-pods.amazonaws.com service principal are shown. If you do not see any roles listed here, you must create one. For more information, see Pod execution role. Page 150 \n• For Subnets, choose the subnets to use for your pods. By default, all subnets in your cluster\'s VPC are selected. Only private subnets are supported for pods running on Fargate; you must deselect any public subnets. • For Tags, you can optionally tag your Fargate profile. These tags do not propagate to other resources associated with the profile, such as its pods.  5. On the Configure pods selection page, enter the following information and choose Next. • list text hereFor Namespace, enter a namespace to match for pods, such as kube-system or default. • Add Kubernetes labels to the selector that pods in the specified namespace must have to match the selector. For example, you could add the label infrastructure: fargate to the selector so that only pods in the specified namespace that also have the infrastructure: fargate Kubernetes label match the selector.  6. On the Review and create page, review the information for your Fargate profile and choose Create. Default Value: By default, AWS Fargate is not utilized. .......................................................................................... 165 \n \n \n  Page 5 \nInternal Only - General \nOverview \nAll CIS Benchmarks™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to \nmaintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be \nused in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: \n• Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and \nquickly updating with the latest security patches. \n• End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response \n(EDR), etc.). \n• Logging and monitoring user and system activity. \nIn the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive \ncybersecurity program.  \nImportant Usage Information \nAll Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They \ncan be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of \nmanual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with \nassessment: \n• CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT® Pro Assessor) \n• CIS Benchmarks™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling \nThese tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of \nsystems and applications.  \nNOTE:  Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can \nbe fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL \nRecommendations (Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are \nimportant for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for \naudits.  \nKey Stakeholders \nCybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative \nwithin an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and \nefficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration \nguidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions \nto specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the \nproblematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. \nThese exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing \npurposes. Page 6 \nInternal Only - General \n \nApply the Correct Version of a Benchmark \nBenchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and \napplying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to \nbe incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target \nsystems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed:  \n• Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the \nenvironment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of \nBenchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and \nStand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. \nApplying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. \n• Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, \nbut especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently \nand using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for \nauditing and remediation. \nExceptions \nThe guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not \nrequirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The \nBenchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, \nwith known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the \nImpact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific \nrequirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a \nRecommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend \nthat a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system\'s primary purpose is to \nfunction as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this \nRecommendation for that specific server). \nIn the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and \nacceptable, and should be handled as follows: \n• The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well \ndocumented for audit purposes. \n• A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the \nfuture, if applicable. \n• If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward \nmitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. \nIt is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and \nwhich settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for \nthe organization. Page 7 \nInternal Only - General \nRemediation \nCIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of \nhardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark\'s \n“Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make \nthat Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. \nWhen remediating systems (changing configuration settings on \ndeployed systems as per the Benchmark\'s Recommendations), \nplease approach this with caution and test thoroughly. \nThe following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: \n• CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be \napplied to production systems without proper testing. \n• Proper testing consists of the following: \no Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted \nsystems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations \n(e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). \no Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if \nthere might be an issue with the targeted systems. \no Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues \narise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production \nsystems. \no When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production \nsystems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be \nresolved prior to deploying more broadly. \no When the initial deployment above is completes successfully, iteratively \ndeploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this \nprocess until the full deployment is complete.  \nSummary \nUsing the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being \nselective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible \nto harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe \nmanner. \nNOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks™ are \navailable for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats \nof the CIS Benchmarks™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for \nCIS SecureSuite® members. \nCIS-CAT® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite® members. This benchmark only includes \ncontrols which can be modified by an end user of Amazon EKS. \nTo obtain the latest version of this guide, please visit www.cisecurity.org. Hence, this document is not scoped for Amazon EKS on AWS Fargate \ncustomers. \n \n  Page 9 \nInternal Only - General \nConsensus Guidance \nThis CIS Benchmark™ was created using a consensus review process comprised of a \nglobal community of subject matter experts. The process combines real world \nexperience with data-based information to create technology specific guidance to assist \nusers to secure their environments. Consensus participants provide perspective from a \ndiverse set of backgrounds including consulting, software development, audit and \ncompliance, security research, operations, government, and legal.  \nEach CIS Benchmark undergoes two phases of consensus review. The first phase \noccurs during initial Benchmark development. During this phase, subject matter experts \nconvene to discuss, create, and test working drafts of the Benchmark. This discussion \noccurs until consensus has been reached on Benchmark recommendations. The \nsecond phase begins after the Benchmark has been published. During this phase, all \nfeedback provided by the Internet community is reviewed by the consensus team for \nincorporation in the Benchmark. If you are interested in participating in the consensus \nprocess, please visit https://workbench.cisecurity.org/. \n  Page 10 \nInternal Only - General \nTypographical Conventions \nThe following typographical conventions are used throughout this guide: \nConvention Meaning \nStylized Monospace font \nUsed for blocks of code, command, and \nscript examples. Text should be interpreted \nexactly as presented. \nMonospace font \nUsed for inline code, commands, UI/Menu \nselections or examples. Text should be \ninterpreted exactly as presented. \n<Monospace font in brackets> Text set in angle brackets denote a variable \nrequiring substitution for a real value. \nItalic font \nUsed to reference other relevant settings, \nCIS Benchmarks and/or Benchmark \nCommunities. Also, used to denote the title \nof a book, article, or other publication. \nBold font \nAdditional information or caveats things like \nNotes, Warnings, or Cautions (usually just \nthe word itself and the rest of the text \nnormal). \n Page 11 \nInternal Only - General \nRecommendation Definitions \nThe following defines the various components included in a CIS recommendation as \napplicable.  If any of the components are not applicable it will be noted, or the \ncomponent will not be included in the recommendation.    \nTitle \nConcise description for the recommendation\'s intended configuration.  \nAssessment Status \nAn assessment status is included for every recommendation. The assessment status \nindicates whether the given recommendation can be automated or requires manual \nsteps to implement. Both statuses are equally important and are determined and \nsupported as defined below:  \nAutomated \nRepresents recommendations for which assessment of a technical control can be fully \nautomated and validated to a pass/fail state. Recommendations will include the \nnecessary information to implement automation. \nManual \nRepresents recommendations for which assessment of a technical control cannot be \nfully automated and requires all or some manual steps to validate that the configured \nstate is set as expected. The expected state can vary depending on the environment. \nProfile \nA collection of recommendations for securing a technology or a supporting platform. \nMost benchmarks include at least a Level 1 and Level 2 Profile. Level 2 extends Level 1 \nrecommendations and is not a standalone profile. The Profile Definitions section in the \nbenchmark provides the definitions as they pertain to the recommendations included for \nthe technology.  \nDescription \nDetailed information pertaining to the setting with which the recommendation is \nconcerned. In some cases, the description will include the recommended value. \nRationale Statement \nDetailed reasoning for the recommendation to provide the user a clear and concise \nunderstanding on the importance of the recommendation. Page 12 \nInternal Only - General \nImpact Statement  \nAny security, functionality, or operational consequences that can result from following \nthe recommendation. \nAudit Procedure  \nSystematic instructions for determining if the target system complies with the \nrecommendation. \nRemediation Procedure \nSystematic instructions for applying recommendations to the target system to bring it \ninto compliance according to the recommendation. \nDefault Value \nDefault value for the given setting in this recommendation, if known. If not known, either \nnot configured or not defined will be applied.  \nReferences \nAdditional documentation relative to the recommendation.  \nCIS Critical Security Controls® (CIS Controls®) \nThe mapping between a recommendation and the CIS Controls is organized by CIS \nControls version, Safeguard, and Implementation Group (IG). The Benchmark in its \nentirety addresses the CIS Controls safeguards of (v7) “5.1 - Establish Secure \nConfigurations” and (v8) \'4.1 - Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process” \nso individual recommendations will not be mapped to these safeguards. \nAdditional Information  \nSupplementary information that does not correspond to any other field but may be \nuseful to the user.  \n \n  Page 13 \nInternal Only - General \nProfile Definitions  \nThe following configuration profiles are defined by this Benchmark: \n• Level 1 \nLevel 1 Configuration Profile \n• Level 2 \nExtends Level 1 \n \n \n  Page 14 \nInternal Only - General \n \n \nAcknowledgements \nThis Benchmark exemplifies the great things a community of users, vendors, and \nsubject matter experts can accomplish through consensus collaboration. The \nshared responsibility model describes this as security of the cloud and security in the \ncloud: \nSecurity of the cloud – AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs \nAWS services in the AWS Cloud. For Amazon EKS, AWS is responsible for the \nKubernetes control plane, which includes the control plane nodes and etcd database. \nThird-party auditors regularly test and verify the effectiveness of our security as part of \nthe AWS compliance programs. To learn about the compliance programs that apply to \nAmazon EKS, see AWS Services in Scope by Compliance Program. \nSecurity in the cloud – Your responsibility includes the following areas. \n• The security configuration of the data plane, including the configuration of the \nsecurity groups that allow traffic to pass from the Amazon EKS control plane into \nthe customer VPC \n• The configuration of the worker nodes and the containers themselves \n• The worker node guest operating system (including updates and security \npatches) \no Amazon EKS follows the shared responsibility model for CVEs and \nsecurity patches on managed node groups. Because managed nodes run \nthe Amazon EKS-optimized AMIs, Amazon EKS is responsible for building \npatched versions of these AMIs when bugs or issues are reported and we \nare able to publish a fix. However, customers are responsible for \ndeploying these patched AMI versions to your managed node groups. \n• Other associated application software: \no Setting up and managing network controls, such as firewall rules \no Managing platform-level identity and access management, either with or in \naddition to IAM \n• The sensitivity of your data, your company’s requirements, and applicable laws \nand regulations \nAWS is responsible for securing the control plane, though you might be able to \nconfigure certain options based on your requirements. Section 2 of this Benchmark \naddresses these configurations. \n2 Control Plane Configuration \nThis section contains recommendations for Amazon EKS control plane logging \nconfiguration. Customers are able to configure logging for control plane in Amazon \nEKS. Page 16 \nInternal Only - General \n2.1 Logging Page 17 \nInternal Only - General \n2.1.1 Enable audit Logs (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nControl plane logs provide visibility into operation of the EKS Control plane component \nsystems. The API server audit logs record all accepted and rejected requests in the \ncluster. When enabled via EKS configuration the control plane logs for a cluster are \nexported to a CloudWatch Log Group for persistence. \nRationale: \nAudit logs enable visibility into all API server requests from authentic and anonymous \nsources. Stored log data can be analyzed manually or with tools to identify and \nunderstand anomalous or negative activity and lead to intelligent remediations. \nImpact: \nEnabling control plane logs, including API server audit logs for Amazon EKS clusters, \nsignificantly strengthens our security posture by providing detailed visibility into all API \nrequests, thereby reducing our attack surface. By exporting these logs to a CloudWatch \nLog Group, we ensure persistent storage and facilitate both manual and automated \nanalysis to quickly identify and remediate anomalous activities. While this configuration \nmight slightly impact usability or performance due to the overhead of logging, the \nenhanced security and compliance benefits far outweigh these drawbacks, making it a \ncritical component of our security strategy. \nAudit: \nFrom Console: \n1. For each EKS Cluster in each region; \n2. Go to \'Amazon EKS\' > \'Clusters\' > \'CLUSTER_NAME\' > \'Configuration\' > \n\'Logging\'. \n3. This will show the control plane logging configuration: \nAPI server: Enabled / Disabled  \nAudit: Enabled / Disabled  \nAuthenticator: Enabled / Disabled \nController manager: Enabled / Disabled \nScheduler: Enabled / Disabled \n \n4. Ensure that all options are set to \'Enabled\'. \nFrom CLI: Page 18 \nInternal Only - General \n# For each EKS Cluster in each region; \nexport CLUSTER_NAME=<your cluster name> \nexport REGION_CODE=<your region_code> \naws eks describe-cluster --name ${CLUSTER_NAME} --region ${REGION_CODE} --\nquery \'cluster.logging.clusterLogging\' \nRemediation: \nFrom Console: \n1. For each EKS Cluster in each region; \n2. Go to \'Amazon EKS\' > \'Clusters\' > \'\' > \'Configuration\' > \'Logging\'. \n3. Click \'Manage logging\'. \n4. Ensure that all options are toggled to \'Enabled\'. \nAPI server: Enabled \nAudit: Enabled  \nAuthenticator: Enabled \nController manager: Enabled \nScheduler: Enabled \n \n5. Click \'Save Changes\'. \nFrom CLI: \n# For each EKS Cluster in each region; \naws eks update-cluster-config \\ \n    --region \'${REGION_CODE}\' \\ \n    --name \'${CLUSTER_NAME}\' \\ \n    --logging \n\'{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator","controllerManage\nr","scheduler"],"enabled":true}]}\' \nDefault Value: \nControl Plane Logging is disabled by default. \nAPI server: Disabled  \nAudit: Disabled  \nAuthenticator: Disabled \nController manager: Disabled \nScheduler: Disabled \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug-application-cluster/audit/ \n2. https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/detective/ \n3. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/control-plane-logs.html \n4. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html Page 19 \nInternal Only - General \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n8.1 Establish and Maintain an Audit Log Management \nProcess \n Establish and maintain an audit log management process that defines the \nenterprise’s logging requirements. Page 23 \nInternal Only - General \n3.1 Worker Node Configuration Files \nThis section covers recommendations for configuration files on Amazon EKS worker \nnodes. Page 24 \nInternal Only - General \n3.1.1 Ensure that the kubeconfig file permissions are set to 644 or \nmore restrictive (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nIf kubelet is running, and if it is configured by a kubeconfig file, ensure that the proxy \nkubeconfig file has permissions of 644 or more restrictive. \nRationale: \nThe kubelet kubeconfig file controls various parameters of the kubelet service in the \nworker node. You should restrict its file permissions to maintain the integrity of the file. \nThe file should be writable by only the administrators on the system. \nIt is possible to run kubelet with the kubeconfig parameters configured as a \nKubernetes ConfigMap instead of a file. In this case, there is no proxy kubeconfig file. \nImpact: \nEnsuring that the kubeconfig file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive \nsignificantly strengthens the security posture of the Kubernetes environment by \npreventing unauthorized modifications. This restricts write access to the kubeconfig file, \nensuring only administrators can alter crucial kubelet configurations, thereby reducing \nthe risk of malicious alterations that could compromise the cluster\'s integrity. \nHowever, this configuration may slightly impact usability, as it limits the ability for non-\nadministrative users to make quick adjustments to the kubelet settings. Administrators \nwill need to balance security needs with operational flexibility, potentially requiring \nadjustments to workflows for managing kubelet configurations. \nAudit: \nMethod 1 \nSSH to the worker nodes \nTo check to see if the Kubelet Service is running: \nsudo systemctl status kubelet \nThe output should return Active: active (running) since.. \nRun the following command on each node to find the appropriate kubeconfig file: \nps -ef | grep kubelet \nThe output of the above command should return something similar to --kubeconfig \n/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig which is the location of the kubeconfig file. \nRun this command to obtain the kubeconfig file permissions: Page 25 \nInternal Only - General \nstat -c %a /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig \nThe output of the above command gives you the kubeconfig file\'s permissions. \nVerify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive. \nMethod 2 \nCreate and Run a Privileged Pod. \nYou will need to run a pod that is privileged enough to access the host\'s file system. \nThis can be achieved by deploying a pod that uses the hostPath volume to mount the \nnode\'s file system into the pod. \nHere\'s an example of a simple pod definition that mounts the root of the host to /host \nwithin the pod: \napiVersion: v1 \nkind: Pod \nmetadata: \n  name: file-check \nspec: \n  volumes: \n  - name: host-root \n    hostPath: \n      path: / \n      type: Directory \n  containers: \n  - name: nsenter \n    image: busybox \n    command: ["sleep", "3600"] \n    volumeMounts: \n    - name: host-root \n      mountPath: /host \n    securityContext: \n      privileged: true \nSave this to a file (e.g., file-check-pod.yaml) and create the pod: \nkubectl apply -f file-check-pod.yaml \nOnce the pod is running, you can exec into it to check file permissions on the node: \nkubectl exec -it file-check -- sh \nNow you are in a shell inside the pod, but you can access the node\'s file system through \nthe /host directory and check the permission level of the file: \nls -l /host/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig \nVerify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive. \nRemediation: \nRun the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker \nnode. For example, Page 26 \nInternal Only - General \nchmod 644 <kubeconfig file> \nDefault Value: \nSee the AWS EKS documentation for the default value. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/kube-proxy/ \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n3.3 Configure Data Access Control Lists \n Configure data access control lists based on a user’s need to know. Apply data \naccess control lists, also known as access permissions, to local and remote file \nsystems, databases, and applications. \n● ● ● \nv7 \n5.2 Maintain Secure Images \n Maintain secure images or templates for all systems in the enterprise based on \nthe organization\'s approved configuration standards. Any new system deployment \nor existing system that becomes compromised should be imaged using one of \nthose images or templates. \n ● ● \n Page 27 \nInternal Only - General \n3.1.2 Ensure that the kubelet kubeconfig file ownership is set to \nroot:root (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nIf kubelet is running, ensure that the file ownership of its kubeconfig file is set to \nroot:root. \nRationale: \nThe kubeconfig file for kubelet controls various parameters for the kubelet service in \nthe worker node. Verify that \nthe ownership is set to root:root. \nRemediation: \nRun the below command (based on the file location on your system) on each worker \nnode. \nFor example, \nchown root:root <proxy kubeconfig file> \nDefault Value: \nSee the AWS EKS documentation for the default value. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/kube-proxy/ Page 29 \nInternal Only - General \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n3.3 Configure Data Access Control Lists \n Configure data access control lists based on a user’s need to know. Apply data \naccess control lists, also known as access permissions, to local and remote file \nsystems, databases, and applications. \n● ● ● \nv7 \n5.2 Maintain Secure Images \n Maintain secure images or templates for all systems in the enterprise based on \nthe organization\'s approved configuration standards. Any new system deployment \nor existing system that becomes compromised should be imaged using one of \nthose images or templates. \n ● ● \n Page 30 \nInternal Only - General \n3.1.3 Ensure that the kubelet configuration file has permissions \nset to 644 or more restrictive (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nEnsure that if the kubelet refers to a configuration file with the --config argument, that \nfile has permissions of 644 or more restrictive. \nRationale: \nThe kubelet reads various parameters, including security settings, from a config file \nspecified by the --config argument. If this file is specified you should restrict its file \npermissions to maintain the integrity of the file. Page 64 \nInternal Only - General \n4.1 RBAC and Service Accounts Page 65 \nInternal Only - General \n4.1.1 Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where \nrequired (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nThe RBAC role cluster-admin provides wide-ranging powers over the environment \nand should be used only where and when needed. \nRationale: \nKubernetes provides a set of default roles where RBAC is used. Some of these roles \nsuch as cluster-admin provide wide-ranging privileges which should only be applied \nwhere absolutely necessary. Roles such as cluster-admin allow super-user access to \nperform any action on any resource. When used in a ClusterRoleBinding, it gives full \ncontrol over every resource in the cluster and in all namespaces. When used in a \nRoleBinding, it gives full control over every resource in the rolebinding\'s namespace, \nincluding the namespace itself. \nImpact: \nCare should be taken before removing any clusterrolebindings from the \nenvironment to ensure they were not required for operation of the cluster. Specifically, \nmodifications should not be made to clusterrolebindings with the system: prefix as \nthey are required for the operation of system components. \nAudit: \nObtain a list of the principals who have access to the cluster-admin role by reviewing \nthe clusterrolebinding output for each role binding that has access to the cluster-\nadmin role. \nkubectl get clusterrolebindings -o=custom-\ncolumns=NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECT:.subjects[*].name \nReview each principal listed and ensure that cluster-admin privilege is required for it. \nRemediation: \nIdentify all clusterrolebindings to the cluster-admin role. Check if they are used and if \nthey need this role or if they could use a role with fewer privileges. \nWhere possible, first bind users to a lower privileged role and then remove the \nclusterrolebinding to the cluster-admin role : Page 66 \nInternal Only - General \nkubectl delete clusterrolebinding [name] \nDefault Value: \nBy default a single clusterrolebinding called cluster-admin is provided with the \nsystem:masters group as its principal. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/authorization/rbac/#user-facing-roles \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n5.4 Restrict Administrator Privileges to Dedicated \nAdministrator Accounts \n Restrict administrator privileges to dedicated administrator accounts on \nenterprise assets. It is possible to set either of \nthese to be the wildcard "*" which matches all items. \nUse of wildcards is not optimal from a security perspective as it may allow for \ninadvertent access to be granted when new resources are added to the Kubernetes API \neither as CRDs or in later versions of the product. \nRationale: \nThe principle of least privilege recommends that users are provided only the access \nrequired for their role and nothing more. General \n4.1.5 Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used. \n(Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nThe default service account should not be used to ensure that rights granted to \napplications can be more easily audited and reviewed. \nRationale: \nKubernetes provides a default service account which is used by cluster workloads \nwhere no specific service account is assigned to the pod. \nWhere access to the Kubernetes API from a pod is required, a specific service account \nshould be created for that pod, and rights granted to that service account. \nThe default service account should be configured such that it does not provide a service \naccount token and does not have any explicit rights assignments. \nImpact: \nAll workloads which require access to the Kubernetes API will require an explicit service \naccount to be created. \nAudit: \nFor each namespace in the cluster, review the rights assigned to the default service \naccount and ensure that it has no roles or cluster roles bound to it apart from the \ndefaults. \nAdditionally ensure that the automountServiceAccountToken: false setting is in \nplace for each default service account. \nRemediation: \nCreate explicit service accounts wherever a Kubernetes workload requires specific \naccess to the Kubernetes API server. \nModify the configuration of each default service account to include this value \nautomountServiceAccountToken: false \nAutomatic remediation for the default account: \nkubectl patch serviceaccount default -p \n$\'automountServiceAccountToken: false\' Page 74 \nInternal Only - General \nDefault Value: \nBy default the default service account allows for its service account token to be \nmounted in pods in its namespace. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-\naccount/ \n2. https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/iam/#disable-auto-mounting-of-\nservice-account-tokens \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n5.3 Disable Dormant Accounts \n Delete or disable any dormant accounts after a period of 45 days of inactivity, \nwhere supported. \n● ● ● \nv7 \n4.3 Ensure the Use of Dedicated Administrative Accounts \n Ensure that all users with administrative account access use a dedicated or \nsecondary account for elevated activities. General \n4.1.6 Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted \nwhere necessary (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nService accounts tokens should not be mounted in pods except where the workload \nrunning in the pod explicitly needs to communicate with the API server \nRationale: \nMounting service account tokens inside pods can provide an avenue for privilege \nescalation attacks where an attacker is able to compromise a single pod in the cluster. \nAvoiding mounting these tokens removes this attack avenue. \nImpact: \nPods mounted without service account tokens will not be able to communicate with the \nAPI server, except where the resource is available to unauthenticated principals. \nAudit: \nReview pod and service account objects in the cluster and ensure that the option below \nis set, unless the resource explicitly requires this access. \nautomountServiceAccountToken: false \nRemediation: \nRegularly review pod and service account objects in the cluster to ensure that the \nautomountServiceAccountToken setting is false for pods and accounts that do not \nexplicitly require API server access. \nDefault Value: \nBy default, all pods get a service account token mounted in them. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-\naccount/ Page 76 \nInternal Only - General \n4.1.7 Cluster Access Manager API to streamline and enhance the \nmanagement of access controls within EKS clusters (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nAmazon EKS has introduced the Cluster Access Manager API to streamline and \nenhance the management of access controls within EKS clusters. This new approach is \nnow the recommended method over the traditional aws-auth ConfigMap for managing \nRole-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Service Accounts. \nKey Advantages of Using the Cluster Access Manager API: \n1. Simplified Access Management: The Cluster Access Manager API allows \nadministrators to manage access directly through the Amazon EKS API, \neliminating the need to modify the aws-auth ConfigMap manually. This reduces \noperational overhead and minimizes the risk of misconfigurations. \n2. Enhanced Security Controls: With this API, administrators can assign \npredefined AWS-managed Kubernetes permissions, known as "access policies," \nto IAM principals. This provides a more secure and auditable way to manage \npermissions compared to manual ConfigMap edits. \n3. Improved Visibility and Auditing: The API offers better visibility into cluster \naccess configurations, facilitating easier auditing and compliance checks. \nAdministrators can list and describe access entries and policies directly through \nthe EKS API. \nRationale: \nThe compelling rationale for using the Cluster Access Manager API instead of the \ntraditional aws-auth ConfigMap in Amazon EKS revolves around security, scalability, \noperational efficiency, and simplified management. \n1. Increased Security and Reduced Risk \n• Direct Management via API: The Cluster Access Manager API enables you to \nmanage RBAC and IAM permissions directly through the EKS API rather than \nediting a ConfigMap. This eliminates the risk of inadvertent errors when manually \nmodifying the aws-auth ConfigMap. \n• Immutable Access Entries: The API ensures that once access entries are \ndefined, they are tightly controlled, reducing the risk of accidental overwrites or \nmisconfigurations that can happen when editing YAML files. \n• Fine-Grained Access Control: By leveraging the new API, you can define access \npolicies at a more granular level than the previous method. This ensures that \nonly the necessary permissions are granted, minimizing the attack surface. Page 78 \nInternal Only - General \n2. Operational Efficiency and Scalability \n• Scalability: Managing access control through the aws-auth ConfigMap becomes \nincreasingly challenging as the number of users and services grows. The new \nAPI scales better by allowing access management through standard AWS \nIdentity and Access Management (IAM) tools. \n• Reduced Operational Overhead: The API simplifies the management of access \ncontrols by removing the need for manual updates to the ConfigMap, reducing \nthe risk of human error, and automating access provisioning through \nInfrastructure as Code (IaC) tools like Terraform or CloudFormation. \n3. Improved Visibility, Auditing, and Compliance \n• Auditable and Traceable Changes: The Cluster Access Manager API integrates \nwith AWS CloudTrail, allowing you to track who made changes to access \nconfigurations. This level of visibility is critical for organizations that need to \nadhere to compliance frameworks like SOC 2, GDPR, or HIPAA. \n• Centralized Management: Unlike the aws-auth ConfigMap, which is managed at \nthe Kubernetes level, the new API leverages AWS IAM’s centralized \nmanagement and auditing capabilities, providing a unified view of access \ncontrols across your AWS environment. \n4. Faster and Safer Access Provisioning \n• No More Cluster Downtime: Errors in the aws-auth ConfigMap can accidentally \nlock out users or admins from the cluster, requiring complex recovery processes. \nThe API-based approach is more resilient, reducing the risk of misconfigurations \ncausing downtime. \n• Immediate Effect: Changes made via the API take effect immediately, whereas \nupdates to the aws-auth ConfigMap may require a delay or even restarting \ncomponents in some cases. \n5. Future-Proofing and Alignment with AWS Best Practices \n• Native Support in Kubernetes Versions: Starting from Kubernetes 1.23, the \nCluster Access Manager API is fully supported and designed to replace the aws-\nauth ConfigMap method. This aligns with AWS’s roadmap and best practices for \nEKS, ensuring your infrastructure remains compatible with future updates. \n• Modern Approach for Pod Identity: When combined with IAM Roles for Service \nAccounts (IRSA) or the new Pod Identity feature, the API supports a more \ndynamic and secure model for assigning permissions to pods, making it easier to \nimplement least-privilege access. Page 79 \nInternal Only - General \nImpact: \nThe shift to using the Cluster Access Manager API instead of the aws-auth ConfigMap \nimpacts EKS RBAC and Service Accounts by simplifying access control management, \nreducing the risk of misconfigurations, and enhancing security. It allows for more \ngranular, direct management of IAM permissions and Kubernetes roles, eliminating \nmanual ConfigMap edits and reducing operational overhead. For Service Accounts, it \nbetter integrates with existing mechanisms like IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) \nfor secure pod access to AWS resources, making it easier to enforce least-privilege \nprinciples. This transition improves scalability, auditing, and compliance, while providing \na future-proof solution aligned with AWS’s Kubernetes identity management roadmap. \nAudit: \nTo check if the Cluster Access Manager API is active on your Amazon EKS cluster, you \ncan use the following AWS CLI command: \naws eks describe-cluster --name $CLUSTER_NAME --query \n"cluster.accessConfig" --output json \nReplace $CLUSTER_NAME with the name of your EKS cluster. \nThe command queries the cluster.accessConfig property, which indicates the \nauthentication mode of the cluster. \nPossible Outputs: \nIf the output shows "authenticationmode": "API" or "authenticationmode": \n"API_AND_CONFIG_MAP", it means the Cluster Access Manager API is enabled. \nIf it only shows "authenticationmode": "CONFIG_MAP", then the cluster is still using \nthe traditional aws-auth ConfigMap approach. \nRemediation: \nLog in to the AWS Management Console. \nNavigate to Amazon EKS and select your EKS cluster. \nGo to the Access tab and click on "Manage Access" in the "Access Configuration \nsection". \nUnder Cluster Authentication Mode for Cluster Access settings. \n• Click EKS API to change cluster will source authenticated IAM \nprincipals only from EKS access entry APIs. \n• Click ConfigMap to change cluster will source authenticated IAM \nprincipals only from the aws-auth ConfigMap. \n• Note: EKS API and ConfigMap must be selected during Cluster creation and \ncannot be changed once the Cluster is provisioned. \nDefault Value: \nEKS API is selected by default during EKS Cluster creation but can be changed during \ninitial configuration Page 80 \nInternal Only - General \n4.1.8 Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate \npermissions in the Kubernetes cluster (Manual) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nCluster roles and roles with the impersonate, bind or escalate permissions should not \nbe granted unless strictly required. Each of these permissions allow a particular subject \nto escalate their privileges beyond those explicitly granted by cluster administrators \nRationale: \nThe impersonate privilege allows a subject to impersonate other users gaining their \nrights to the cluster. The bind privilege allows the subject to add a binding to a cluster \nrole or role which escalates their effective permissions in the cluster. The escalate \nprivilege allows a subject to modify cluster roles to which they are bound, increasing \ntheir rights to that level. \nEach of these permissions has the potential to allow for privilege escalation to cluster-\nadmin level. \nImpact: \nThere are some cases where these permissions are required for cluster service \noperation, and care should be taken before removing these permissions from system \nservice accounts. \nAudit: \nReview the users who have access to cluster roles or roles which provide the \nimpersonate, bind or escalate privileges. \nRemediation: \nWhere possible, remove the impersonate, bind and escalate rights from subjects. \nDefault Value: \nIn a default kubeadm cluster, the system:masters group and clusterrole-aggregation-\ncontroller service account have access to the escalate privilege. The system:masters \ngroup also has access to bind and impersonate. \nReferences: \n1. https://www.impidio.com/blog/kubernetes-rbac-security-pitfalls \n2. https://raesene.github.io/blog/2020/12/12/Escalating_Away/ \n3. https://raesene.github.io/blog/2021/01/16/Getting-Into-A-Bind-with-Kubernetes/ Page 82 \nInternal Only - General \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n4.8 Uninstall or Disable Unnecessary Services on \nEnterprise Assets and Software \n Uninstall or disable unnecessary services on enterprise assets and software, \nsuch as an unused file sharing service, web application module, or service \nfunction. \n ● ● \nv7 \n14.7 Enforce Access Control to Data through Automated \nTools \n Use an automated tool, such as host-based Data Loss Prevention, to enforce \naccess controls to data even when data is copied off a system. \n  ● \n Page 83 \nInternal Only - General \n4.2 Pod Security Standards \nPod Security Standards (PSS) are recommendations for securing deployed workloads \nto reduce the risks of container breakout. There are a number of ways if implementing \nPSS, including the built-in Pod Security Admission controller, or external policy control \nsystems which integrate with Kubernetes via validating and mutating webhooks. \nThe previous feature described in this document, pod security policy (preview), was \ndeprecated with version 1.21, and removed as of version 1.25. After pod security policy \n(preview) is deprecated, you must disable the feature on any existing clusters using the \ndeprecated feature to perform future cluster upgrades and stay within Azure support. Page 84 \nInternal Only - General \n4.2.1 Minimize the admission of privileged containers (Automated) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nDo not generally permit containers to be run with the securityContext.privileged \nflag set to true. \nRationale: \nPrivileged containers have access to all Linux Kernel capabilities and devices. A \ncontainer running with full privileges can do almost everything that the host can do. This \nflag exists to allow special use-cases, like manipulating the network stack and \naccessing devices. \nThere should be at least one admission control policy defined which does not permit \nprivileged containers. \nIf you need to run privileged containers, this should be defined in a separate policy and \nyou should carefully check to ensure that only limited service accounts and users are \ngiven permission to use that policy. \nImpact: \nPods defined with spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: true, \nspec.initContainers[].securityContext.privileged: true and \nspec.ephemeralContainers[].securityContext.privileged: true will not be \npermitted. Page 85 \nInternal Only - General \nAudit: \nList the policies in use for each namespace in the cluster, ensure that each policy \ndisallows the admission of privileged containers. \nSince manually searching through each pod\'s configuration might be tedious, especially \nin environments with many pods, you can use a more automated approach with grep or \nother command-line tools. \nHere\'s an example of how you might approach this with a combination of kubectl, grep, \nand shell scripting for a more automated solution: \nkubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r \'.items[] | \nselect(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged == true) | \n.metadata.name\' \nOR \nkubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq \'.items[] | \nselect(.metadata.namespace != "kube-system" and \n.spec.containers[]?.securityContext?.privileged == true) | {pod: \n.metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, container: \n.spec.containers[].name}\' \nWhen creating a Pod Security Policy, ["kube-system"] namespaces are excluded by \ndefault. \nThis command uses jq, a command-line JSON processor, to parse the JSON output \nfrom kubectl get pods and filter out pods where any container has the \nsecurityContext.privileged flag set to true. Please note that you might need to adjust the \ncommand depending on your specific requirements and the structure of your pod \nspecifications. \nRemediation: \nAdd policies to each namespace in the cluster which has user workloads to restrict the \nadmission of privileged containers. \nTo enable PSA for a namespace in your cluster, set the pod-\nsecurity.kubernetes.io/enforce label with the policy value you want to enforce. \nkubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod-\nsecurity.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \nThe above command enforces the restricted policy for the NAMESPACE namespace. \nYou can also enable Pod Security Admission for all your namespaces. For example: \nkubectl label --overwrite ns --all pod-\nsecurity.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline \nDefault Value: \nBy default, there are no restrictions on the creation of privileged containers. \nReferences: \n1. https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-admission/ \n2. https://aws.github.io/aws-eks-best-practices/pods/#restrict-the-containers-that-\ncan-run-as-privileged Page 86 \nInternal Only - General \nCIS Controls: \nControls \nVersion Control IG 1 IG 2 IG 3 \nv8 \n5.4 Restrict Administrator Privileges to Dedicated \nAdministrator Accounts \n Restrict administrator privileges to dedicated administrator accounts on \nenterprise assets. Allowing this right can lead to a process running a container getting more \nrights than it started with. \nIt\'s important to note that these rights are still constrained by the overall container \nsandbox, and this setting does not relate to the use of privileged containers. \nRationale: \nA container running with the allowPrivilegeEscalation flag set to true may have \nprocesses that can gain more privileges than their parent. \nThere should be at least one admission control policy defined which does not permit \ncontainers to allow privilege escalation. The option exists (and is defaulted to true) to \npermit setuid binaries to run. \nIf you have need to run containers which use setuid binaries or require privilege \nescalation, this should be defined in a separate policy and you should carefully check to \nensure that only limited service accounts and users are given permission to use that \npolicy. \nImpact: \nPods defined with spec.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true will not be permitted \nunless they are run under a specific policy. Page 94 \nInternal Only - General \nAudit: \nList the policies in use for each namespace in the cluster, ensure that each policy \ndisallows the admission of containers which allow privilege escalation. \nThis command gets all pods across all namespaces, outputs their details in JSON \nformat, and uses jq to parse and filter the output for containers with \nallowPrivilegeEscalation set to true. \nkubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r \'.items[] | \nselect(any(.spec.containers[]; \n.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == true)) | \n"\\(.metadata.namespace)/\\(.metadata.name)"\' \nOR \nkubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq \'.items[] | \nselect(.metadata.namespace != "kube-system" and .spec.containers[]; \n.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == true) | {pod: \n.metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, container: \n.spec.containers[].name}\' \nWhen creating a Pod Security Policy, ["kube-system"] namespaces are excluded by \ndefault. \nThis command uses jq, a command-line JSON processor, to parse the JSON output \nfrom kubectl get pods and filter out pods where any container has the \nsecurityContext.privileged flag set to true. Page 107 \nInternal Only - General \n4.5.1 Create administrative boundaries between resources using \nnamespaces (Manual) \nProfile Applicability: \n•  Level 1 \nDescription: \nUse namespaces to isolate your Kubernetes objects. \nRationale: \nLimiting the scope of user permissions can reduce the impact of mistakes or malicious \nactivities. Amazon \nECR supports specific actions, resources, and condition keys. To learn about all of the \nelements that you use in a JSON policy, see IAM JSON Policy Elements Reference in \nthe IAM User Guide. \nActions \nThe Action element of an IAM identity-based policy describes the specific action or \nactions that will be allowed or denied by the policy. Policy actions usually have the \nsame name as the associated AWS API operation. The action is used in a policy to \ngrant permissions to perform the associated operation. \nPolicy actions in Amazon ECR use the following prefix before the action: ecr:. For \nexample, to grant someone permission to create an Amazon ECR repository with the \nAmazon ECR CreateRepository API operation, you include the ecr:CreateRepository \naction in their policy. Policy statements must include either an Action or NotAction \nelement. Amazon ECR defines its own set of actions that describe tasks that you can \nperform with this service. \nTo specify multiple actions in a single statement, separate them with commas as \nfollows: \n"Action": [ "ecr:action1", "ecr:action2" \nYou can specify multiple actions using wildcards (*). For example, to specify all actions \nthat begin with the word Describe, include the following action: \n"Action": "ecr:Describe*" \nTo see a list of Amazon ECR actions, see Actions, Resources, and Condition Keys for \nAmazon Elastic Container Registry in the IAM User Guide. \nResources \nThe Resource element specifies the object or objects to which the action applies. \nStatements must include either a Resource or a NotResource element. You specify a \nresource using an ARN or using the wildcard (*) to indicate that the statement applies to \nall resources. \nAn Amazon ECR repository resource has the following ARN: \narn:${Partition}:ecr:${Region}:${Account}:repository/${Repository-\nname} \nFor more information about the format of ARNs, see Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) \nand AWS Service Namespaces. \nFor example, to specify the my-repo repository in the us-east-1 Region in your \nstatement, use the following ARN: \n"Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-1:123456789012:repository/my-repo" \nTo specify all repositories that belong to a specific account, use the wildcard (*): \n"Resource": "arn:aws:ecr:us-east-1:123456789012:repository/*" \nTo specify multiple resources in a single statement, separate the ARNs with commas. \n"Resource": [ "resource1", "resource2" \nTo see a list of Amazon ECR resource types and their ARNs, see Resources Defined \nby Amazon Elastic Container Registry in the IAM User Guide. To learn with which \nactions you can specify the ARN of each resource, see Actions Defined by Amazon \nElastic Container Registry. Page 117 \nInternal Only - General \nCondition Keys \nThe Condition element (or Condition block) lets you specify conditions in which a \nstatement is in effect. The Condition element is optional. You can build conditional \nexpressions that use condition operators, such as equals or less than, to match the \ncondition in the policy with values in the request. \nIf you specify multiple Condition elements in a statement, or multiple keys in a single \nCondition element, AWS evaluates them using a logical AND operation. If you specify \nmultiple values for a single condition key, AWS evaluates the condition using a logical \nOR operation. All of the conditions must be met before the statement\'s permissions are \ngranted. \nYou can also use placeholder variables when you specify conditions. For example, you \ncan grant an IAM user permission to access a resource only if it is tagged with their IAM \nuser name. For more information, see IAM Policy Elements: Variables and Tags in the \nIAM User Guide. \nAmazon ECR defines its own set of condition keys and also supports using some global \ncondition keys.
